newsitem.title: USA: Siebert sees firm as major muni player in 5 years.
newsitem.headline: Siebert sees firm as major muni player in 5 years.

text.p: Brokerage owner Muriel Siebert predicted that her venture with California municipal banker Napolean Brandford would thrive despite the suddenness of her decision to expand her firm's municipal banking operations.

"In five years if I'm lucky, and I think that I will be, we could be a major player in the business," Siebert told Reuters in an interview on Friday. "Not a Goldman, not that capitalized. But a major player."
Siebert, whose firm is capitalized at about $11 million, was in Florida last week to visit the company's new office in Surfside, northeast of Miami.
She said she was the one who approached Brandford after learning his partner, Calvin Grigsby, had resigned from Grigsby Brandford & Co Inc.

Grigsby resigned as company president after newspaper reports said federal agents were investigating allegations he was involved in municipal bond kickbacks. He is not charged with any crime and has since rejoined the firm, now known as Grigsby & Associates.
Siebert said she had long been impressed by the professionalism of the firm, which was the largest black-owned firm in the business.
While concentrating on equities, her firm had moved into municipal bonds on a small scale because its retail customers bought them, Siebert said.
"We have had a muni division but we were geared more toward selling. Our banking capabilities were limited," she said.
The reports of Grigsby's alleged problems forced her hand, she said.

"It happened fast. I was not out looking (to expand muni operations). It was nothing that was driving me because the business is still in rotten shape," Siebert said. "But when you see an opportunity like this you have to do it, an opportunity to hire people who have worked together as a team."
The vast majority of the 35 employees of her firms' Siebert Brandford Shank & Co division are Grigsby Brandford alumni, Siebert said.

The division is still in the process of merging. Some of the Grigsby Brandford hirees have moved into Siebert's office in Los Angeles, while Siebert has taken over former Grigsby-Brandford offices in Chicago and Detroit.
Siebert is considering opening an Atlanta office, and plans to add discount brokers at some of the offices that are now strictly part of the muni division.
Siebert said the division was just appointed senior manager for an Oakland, Calif., deal and senior co-manager in Houston muni issue.

"It's going to take a couple of years before we're solidly in munis and in the deals we want to be," she said. "In some cases it's like starting from scratch. With the old contracts, we have to show them us as a new firm."
Siebert said the new division is the only woman-owned and minority-owned firm. While the nation is shifting away from minority set-aside programs, Siebert said that shouldn't matter.

"As long as there is a sensitivity to diversity and a sense of equality, then the women-owned and African America-owned companies will make it," Siebert said. "As long as we have women and minorities that are elected to office, there should be a sensitivity."
Nor is she worried about expanding municipal banking operations at a time when many other firms are trimming their muni departments.

"The spreads have got to widen," Siebert said. "But there will always be a market for munis. We're going to have to rebuild the infrastrucutre, all the urban cities, and the best way to finance it is still munis."
